Vyasa appeared, explaining that Krishna and Arjuna were incarnations of Narayana and Nara, Ashwatthama was Rudra's incarnation, and all were blessed by Shiva, leading to a ceasefire.
Drona's father, Bharadvaja, saw the celestial nymph Hritachi during a sacrifice, lost control of his passion, and his semen fell into a wooden bowl, from which Drona was born.
Drona grew up in a hermitage studying the Vedas and martial arts, where he became close friends with Drupada, son of King Prishata.
Drupada promised that when he inherited the kingdom, he would share his kingdom and wealth with Drona.
Drupada returned to inherit the kingdom, and Drona married Kripi and had a son named Ashwatthama.
When Parashurama was giving away his possessions to Brahmins, Drona arrived late and received all of Parashurama's divine weapons instead.
Drona went to meet King Drupada, but Drupada rejected their friendship, citing their now unequal status and wealth.
Angered, Drona went to Hastinapura and became the martial arts teacher for the Kaurava and Pandava princes.
Drona asked his students to promise to do one thing for him after mastering their skills; only Arjuna agreed immediately.

Karna is a complex tragic character in the Mahabharata. He was Kunti's illegitimate son with Surya before her marriage.
Kunti, fearing family criticism, secretly placed baby Karna in a basket and abandoned him in the river, praying to gods for his protection.
The basket floated down the river and was found by Radha, wife of the charioteer Adhiratha, who raised Karna as their son.
Kunti never forgot this child and secretly sent spies to find his whereabouts.
Due to his charioteer-son identity, Karna faced many hardships and difficulties in life.
In his youth, Karna studied martial arts under Drona and became friends with Duryodhana.
Seeing Arjuna's martial prowess, Karna asked Drona to teach him the secret of using the Brahmastra, but was refused because Drona said it could only be taught to Brahmins and Kshatriyas.
Karna disguised himself as a Brahmin and learned this art from Parashurama.
One day, Parashurama slept with his head on Karna's thigh. A small insect bit Karna's thigh and sucked blood, but Karna endured the pain without moving to avoid waking his teacher.
Parashurama woke up and, based on Karna's endurance, determined he wasn't a Brahmin. Karna admitted he was a charioteer's son.
Parashurama cursed Karna that the Brahmastra he mastered would not work at critical moments in battle.
During this period, Karna accidentally shot and killed a Brahmin's cow, and the Brahmin cursed him that his chariot wheel would sink into the ground when fighting an opponent.
After completing their martial training, the Kauravas and Pandavas held a martial arts exhibition. Arjuna's skills were outstanding.
At the end of the exhibition, Karna arrived at the field ready to compete with Arjuna.
Seeing this, Kunti fainted.
Teacher Kripa asked Karna to announce his royal lineage. Karna hung his head in shame.
Duryodhana stood up and said if Karna wasn't a prince and thus ineligible to compete, he would now crown Karna as King of Anga.
Karna's charioteer father came to call him back, and Bhima learned Karna was a charioteer's son and mocked him bitterly.

extraction_text: Bhimasena (Bheema) was stronger than the Kauravas in running and wrestling, making Duryodhana jealous.

After the princes grew up and Yudhishthira was favored to become king, Duryodhana convinced Dhritarashtra to send the Pandavas to Varanavata.
Duryodhana built a flammable lacquer palace in Varanavata to burn the Pandavas alive, but they escaped with Vidura's help.
The Pandavas lived in hiding until they revealed themselves at Draupadi's swayamvara in Panchala and married her.
Duryodhana and Karna plotted to attack the Pandavas, but Dhritarashtra, advised by Bhishma, Drona, and Vidura, instead divided the kingdom, giving half to the Pandavas.
The Pandavas built Indraprastha, performed a Rajasuya sacrifice, and became prosperous, increasing Duryodhana's jealousy.
Duryodhana, distressed, threatened suicide, and Shakuni suggested a dice game to defeat Yudhishthira.
Dhritarashtra, pressured by Duryodhana, invited Yudhishthira to gamble in Hastinapura, despite Vidura's objections.
Yudhishthira lost everything in the dice game, and Dushasana dragged Draupadi into the assembly to humiliate her, leading Bhimasena to vow revenge.

Dhritarashtra released the Pandavas after Draupadi's plea, but Duryodhana convinced him to recall Yudhishthira for a second dice game, resulting in the Pandavas' 12-year exile and 1-year incognito period.
During the exile, Duryodhana went to the forest to mock the Pandavas but was captured by Gandharvas and rescued by the Pandavas.
Duryodhana, ashamed, ordered everyone to return to the city and decided to stay there to 'fast to death'.
After repeated persuasion and Karna's assurance of defeating the Pandavas in the future, Duryodhana got up and returned to the city.
Duryodhana, relying on Dhritarashtra's authority from childhood, was arrogant and did as he pleased. He was vain, jealous, and obsessed with seizing the throne.
Dhritarashtra doted on his son and wanted him to inherit the throne, so he could not effectively restrain him and instead let his son manipulate him.
After depriving the Pandavas of their kingdom, Duryodhana became even more emboldened.
When the Pandavas' thirteen-year exile ended and they demanded half the kingdom, Duryodhana arrogantly declared he would not give them even a needlepoint of land.

At the start of the war, the Kaurava army had a clear advantage in military strength, but the war lacked moral justification, so the army lacked unity.
Facing continuous setbacks, Duryodhana was determined to resist to the end, preferring to die on the battlefield rather than seek peace with the Pandavas.

extraction_text: On the last day of the war, Duryodhana fought until the entire Kaurava army was annihilated, then fled the battlefield and hid in a pond.
The Pandavas led their army to the pond and challenged him. Facing reality, Duryodhana admitted defeat and offered to surrender the land.
Yudhishthira insisted on deciding the outcome through combat, so Duryodhana accepted the challenge.
Yudhishthira agreed to a one-on-one mace duel and let Duryodhana choose any opponent from the Pandavas. Duryodhana arrogantly let the Pandavas choose their own representative.
Duryodhana fought Bhima, the most skilled mace fighter among the Pandavas, in a fierce and evenly matched battle.
Following Krishna and Arjuna's instructions, Bhima deliberately violated mace duel rules and broke Duryodhana's legs.
After falling, Duryodhana condemned Krishna for always winning through unlawful means and took pride in dying on the battlefield following Kshatriya dharma.
The Kshatriya warriors in the Mahabharata emphasize combat rules, and Balarama expresses great anger at Bhima for violating the rules of mace fighting.
Duryodhana accuses Krishna of violating combat rules, while Krishna rebuts by linking Duryodhana's entire life of evil deeds.

After falling, Duryodhana tells Sanjaya to convey to his parents that the Pandavas killed him using illegal means, like killing someone asleep or with poison, which inadvertently reveals his own past methods against the Pandavas.
Ashwatthama, Kripa, and Kritavarma leave Duryodhana and rest in a forest near the camp. Ashwatthama, filled with sorrow and anger, cannot sleep.
Ashwatthama sees an owl attack sleeping crows at night, inspiring him to decide to sneak attack the sleeping Pandava army.

Ashwatthama wakes Kripa and Kritavarma to seek their opinion. Kripa argues that killing sleeping people violates combat rules and suggests waiting until morning, but Ashwatthama insists the Pandavas violated rules first by killing his father and others, so he will proceed even if it means rebirth as a worm or moth.
Unable to dissuade him, Kripa and Kritavarma follow Ashwatthama as they set out.
At the camp entrance, Ashwatthama is blocked by a powerful, enormous being. In desperation, he prays to Lord Shiva for protection, offering himself as a sacrifice.
Shiva appears and grants Ashwatthama a sharp sword.
Ashwatthama enters the camp, while Kripa and Kritavarma guard the entrance. He kills all the sleeping Panchala and Pandava warriors in the camp, led by Dhrishtadyumna, including Draupadi's five sons.
The three then go to the dying Duryodhana, and Ashwatthama reports the success of the night attack.
Duryodhana expressed relief before dying, acknowledging that Ashwatthama, Kripa, and Kritavarman achieved what Bhishma, Karna, and Drona could not.
Yudhishthira learned about the night raid and lamented, while Draupadi demanded Ashwatthama's death and his jewel as proof, threatening to fast until death.
